common_name: Spicy Orange Thyme (Orange Spice Groundcover Thyme)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this low, spreading thyme is grown vegetatively since seed does not come true.

directions: Spicy Orange, sometimes sold as Orange Spice thyme, is a low, mat-forming culinary thyme whose crushed foliage releases a bright, sweet-orange scent and flavor distinct from the more balsamic, resinous Orange Balsam cultivar. Its trailing, groundcover habit sets it apart from upright culinary thymes, making it useful for edging paths, tumbling over walls, or filling gaps between pavers where the scent releases underfoot, while pink summer flowers draw bees. Snip fresh sprigs to flavor poultry, fish, or fruit-based glazes, and shear lightly after bloom to keep the mat dense and encourage new tender growth.

planting.note: Direct sow every 2-3 weeks from early spring through summer in full sun; compact, densely branched habit and short internodes suit containers and small beds as well as open ground.

directions: Teddy is a compact dill bred for dense, finely feathered leaf production, with short internodes that pack thick leaflets tightly around each stem for a lush, full appearance even on a small plant. It is faster-growing and more productive for leaf harvest than the older compact standard Fernleaf, while still being slower to bolt than large field-type dills, extending the fresh-cut window. Its small stature makes it well suited to pots, window boxes, and tight garden spaces where a full-size dill would flop or crowd neighbors. Harvest leaves continuously for dill weed; allow a few plants to flower if seed heads are wanted for pickling.

common_name: Extra Curled Dwarf Parsley (Compact Heirloom Curly Parsley)

planting.note: Soak seed before sowing to speed slow, erratic parsley germination; direct sow or start indoors and transplant into rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Extra Curled Dwarf is a French heirloom curly parsley selected for a low, dense, tightly compact habit and finely ruffled, deep-green leaves, making it noticeably shorter and more uniform in the row than taller curly types like Triple Curled or Paramount. Its neat, mounded form suits edging, window boxes, and container plantings where a tall parsley would look leggy, while retaining the same mild, clean parsley flavor prized for garnish and fresh chopping. As a biennial it forms an edible rosette the first year and will bolt to flower and seed in its second season if overwintered in mild climates. Harvest outer leaves continuously to keep the compact rosette productive.

common_name: Genovese Compact, Improved Basil (Uniform Container Pesto Basil)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil once frost danger passes; the compact, uniform habit suits containers and close in-ground spacing alike.

directions: Genovese Compact, Improved carries the same cupped, dark-green, 2-3 inch pesto-type leaves and classic sweet Genovese flavor as standard Genovese basil, but on shorter, more uniform 16-18 inch plants bred for even germination and consistent habit in container and retail production. That compactness and uniformity also make it a reliable choice for home gardeners who want a tidy, productive basil in a pot on a patio or windowsill rather than the taller, more sprawling standard Genovese. Pinch flower spikes regularly to keep leaf production going and delay the flavor decline that comes with flowering. Harvest by cutting stem tips just above a leaf node to encourage bushy regrowth through the season.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes.

directions: Dolly is a high-yielding Genovese-type basil bred for field production, with large, cupped leaves up to 4 inches long that are somewhat lighter green than standard Genovese and lightly serrated at the margin. Plants are notably uniform in habit and leaf shape while remaining somewhat compact for the leaf size, giving good yield per square foot for market growers and home gardeners alike. Flavor is classic sweet basil, suited to pesto, Caprese salads, and general Italian cooking. Pinch out flower spikes to prolong leaf harvest, and cut whole stem tips regularly to keep plants bushy and productive through the season.

common_name: Horapha Nanum Thai Basil (Compact Anise-Clove Thai Basil)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 50F.

directions: Horapha Nanum, nanum meaning dwarf, is a compact, bushy strain of Thai basil, named for horapha, the Thai term for this basil type, that stays noticeably smaller and denser than standard Thai basil selections like Siam Queen. Deep purple-brown stems carry olive-green, purple-tinged, slightly serrated leaves with the same pungent anise-clove flavor prized in Thai and Vietnamese cooking, and its small mulberry-purple flower clusters make it an attractive pot plant as well as a kitchen herb. The dwarf habit suits containers and small raised beds where a full-size Thai basil would sprawl. Pinch flower spikes to extend leaf harvest, and cut stems above a leaf pair to keep the plant branching.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost or root cuttings, and set out after frost danger passes into lean, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Compactum is a dwarf selection of sweet marjoram, staying in a tight, low mound well under the 12-18 inches typical of the species while carrying the same sweet, floral, mildly resinous flavor prized in Mediterranean cooking. Its small scale and neat habit make it well suited to window boxes, edging, and container culture where standard sweet marjoram would grow loose and sprawling. Like the species it is a tender perennial grown as an annual outside USDA zone 9-11, though potted plants can be brought indoors for winter. Pinch tips regularly to keep the mound dense and to delay flowering, which is when leaf flavor is at its peak just before buds open.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Polyvert Chives (Uniform Dark Green Culinary Chive)

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost or direct sow after danger of frost, or plant divisions of an established clump in spring.

directions: Polyvert is a market-garden chive selection bred for highly uniform, medium-sized, dark green leaves that are slightly thinner than those of comparable field varieties, giving an even, tidy stand well suited to bunching for market or steady cutting in the home garden. Flavor is the standard mild, oniony chive taste, good snipped fresh over eggs, potatoes, or salads. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and harvest by cutting leaves an inch or two above the base, which encourages continuous regrowth through the season. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep plants vigorous.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost or direct sow after danger of frost, or plant divisions of an established clump in spring; the upright, fine-leaf habit does well in containers.

directions: Nelly is a fine-to-medium leaf chive with a uniform, upright habit and slender, dark green leaves, a leaf profile favored for bunching and fresh use because it gives a refined, delicate appearance when snipped over a finished dish. It performs well in containers as well as garden beds, making it a good option for a kitchen-window herb pot. Flavor is the classic mild onion taste typical of common chives, and the pale purple pompom flowers that follow are edible and attractive to pollinators if left to bloom. Harvest by snipping leaves near the base regularly to keep the clump producing tender new growth, and divide every few years in spring as clumps become congested.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or root divisions in spring into moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; confine roots in a container or barrier, as with all mints, to prevent spreading.

directions: Todd's Mitcham is an improved strain of the classic Black Mitcham peppermint, released in the 1970s from an irradiation breeding program at Brookhaven National Laboratory specifically to improve field resistance to Verticillium wilt, the disease that devastates commercial mint plantings. It carries the same strong, high-menthol peppermint flavor and aroma prized for tea, confections, and oil distillation as standard Black Mitcham, but with better resilience in soils where wilt has been a problem. Like other peppermints it spreads aggressively by rhizome, so garden plantings should be contained in pots or sunk barriers. Harvest stems just before flowering, when menthol content and flavor peak, for the best fresh or dried leaf.
sources: PMC/NCBI Verticillium Wilt of Mint review
